newsitem.title: USA: Hashimoto's G7 success tempered by trade issue.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto's G7 success tempered by trade issue.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto worked hard to raise Japan's profile here at the Group of Seven summit this weekend but the diplomatic success was tempered by concern about his country's growing trade surplus.
Japan's initiative to send an envoy to Cambodia as a G7 representative was welcomed at the summit by other leaders.

Japanese officials had feared this meeting of the G7 -- which also includes Germany, France, Italy, Britain, the United States and Canada -- would become Euro-centric because of Russia's formal participation.
"Along with French President (Jacques) Chirac and German President (Helmut) Kohl, Hashimoto dominated much of the summit discussion," a senior Japanese government official said.
The offical said Japan had been seen only as an economic power in the past but the initiative on Cambodia proved Tokyo could be a political force, especially in Asian affairs.
Observers said Hashimoto also signalled his eagerness to serve his second two-year term by pledging to visit Russia, German, France and Canada either this year or next.

Political analysts predict that Hashimoto will be reselected as leader of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party at a party election in September which makes his re-election as prime minister a sure thing. Hashimoto has not yet publicly stated his intention to run for the party election.

"Building personal ties between leaders by visiting each other's countries like what European and U.S. leaders are doing among themselves is what Japan has wanted to do," another Japanese offical said. "That will certainly set a stage for smooth sailing in diplomacy at least in the beginning."
But the glow from these efforts at the G7 were dimmed by U.S. criticism of Japan's growing trade surplus with the world and mention of the problem in the G7 leaders' economic statement.
The statement said Japan has the objective of "achieving strong domestic demand-led growth and avoiding a significant increase in its external surplus."
With snowballing budget deficits, Japan is now carrying out drastic fiscal reforms that may dampen domestic demand and widen the trade surplus with the world even further.
President Clinton warned at his closing news conference in Denver that Japan was playing with fire if the trade imbalances continued.
"If we return to a time when we've got exploding trade deficits then that will once again move front and centre into our relationship in a way that won't be good for either country," Clinton said.
But Hashimoto said at his own closing press conference: "I do not think that Japan's trade and services surplus will increase significantly."

The Japanese prime minister also took the opportunity of the G7 summit to raise the issue of disputed islands between Japan and Russia that have blocked the signing of a formal peace treaty ending World War Two hostilities betwen the two countries.
Although no solution was agreed, Russian Prime Minister Boris Yeltsin did make an important gesture by taking Japan off nuclear missile targets.
But here too, hard work lies ahead. Russian spokesman Sergie Yastrzhembsky said Sunday that the North Pacific islands dispute was unlikely to be resolved in this generation.
